key_insight: Machine-learned long-time dynamics show that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move orders of magnitude more slowly than in the bulk because surface hopping pathways are strongly restricted.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can exhibit much lower electron mobility than single-crystal samples and informs surface-engineering strategies for catalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics from bulk oxides to redox-active oxide surfaces
Ran nanosecond-scale simulations across a temperature range on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110)
Analyzed polaron hopping pathways, interlayer events, and vacancy-induced charge redistribution
evidence_signal: The study uses several nanoseconds of finite-temperature dynamics to statistically resolve rare hopping events and quantify the suppression of surface polaron mobility.
watch_item: The approach relies on a trained machine-learning model, so transferability and accuracy must be carefully validated for other oxide surfaces, defect types, and temperature regimes.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
